summary: Describes extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol for setting up point-to-multipoint and multipoint-to-multipoint label switched paths in MPLS networks, known as multipoint LDP. It builds these paths without relying on any other multicast tree protocol.

eli5.summary: Sometimes one sender needs to reach many receivers. This lets MPLS routers build a tree of paths for that using the same protocol they already use for labels.

questions: difference between p2mp and mp2mp lsp
what is make before break in mldp
subtitle: How MPLS routers build one-to-many and many-to-many label switched paths using only LDP.

tldr.problem: LDP could set up point-to-point and multipoint-to-point LSPs, but not paths that deliver traffic from one or many senders to many receivers.
tldr.mechanism: Leaves send label mappings toward the root along the best path, using new P2MP and MP2MP FEC elements identified by a root address and an opaque value. Each router along the way copies packets as the tree branches.
tldr.outcome: MPLS networks can build multipoint LSPs without a multicast protocol, with extras for LANs, root redundancy and make-before-break. It was later updated by RFC 7358.

today: RFC 6388 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7358. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Multipoint LSPs with LDP
sections.content:
LDP (RFC 5036) sets up point-to-point (P2P) and multipoint-to-point (MP2P) label switched paths. RFC 6388 extends it to set up point-to-multipoint (P2MP) and multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) LSPs, together called MP LSPs. A P2MP LSP carries traffic from a single root (ingress) to a number of leaf (egress) nodes. An MP2MP LSP carries traffic from multiple ingress nodes to multiple egress nodes.

Only a single copy of a packet is sent to an LDP neighbor that the MP LSP traverses, and this works without a multicast protocol in the network. Several MP LSPs can be rooted at one ingress node, each with its own identifier.

The design assumes that leaf nodes already know the root and identifier of their MP LSP. How they learn it, and how an application uses the LSP, are out of scope.
sections.eli5: This lets routers set up a tree of roads so one sender can reach many receivers. Each router only sends one copy down each road, and copies are made where the road splits.

sections.title: Roles and Terminology
sections.content:
A P2MP LSP has one ingress LSR, called the root, and one or more egress LSRs. An MP2MP LSP has a distinguished root that connects a set of nodes, so traffic sent by any node is delivered to all the others. A transit LSR has a directly connected upstream LSR toward the root and one or more directly connected downstream LSRs. A bud LSR is an egress that also has downstream neighbors. A leaf in an MP2MP LSP is both ingress and egress.

An FEC (Forwarding Equivalence Class) element here does not necessarily identify the traffic mapped to the LSP, so the RFC calls the term a misnomer. The notation <X, Y> means a path with root address X and opaque value Y.

Leaf nodes initiate setup and tear-down, transit nodes install forwarding state and pass setup toward the root, and the root maps traffic into the LSP. A leaf node finds out its role by a discovery process outside this document.
sections.eli5: The root is the trunk of the tree, the leaves are the houses that get the package, and the routers in between are the branches that pass things along.

sections.title: FEC Elements and Capabilities
sections.content:
The P2MP FEC Element (type 0x06) carries an address family, an address length, the root node address, an opaque length and an opaque value. The root address plus the opaque value uniquely identify a P2MP LSP in the network. If the address family is IPv4 the address length MUST be 4, and for IPv6 it MUST be 16. A mismatch should cause the receiver to abort and send an Unknown FEC notification. The element MUST be the only FEC element in its FEC TLV.

The opaque value is made of LDP MP opaque value elements that transit nodes need not interpret. The basic generic LSP identifier is type 1, length 4, with a 32-bit integer unique in the context of the root. It is recommended when mapping traffic to LSPs is non-algorithmic and done outside LDP. Type 255 introduces an extended type.

MP2MP LSPs reuse the same structure with two FEC types: upstream 0x07 and downstream 0x08. Support is advertised with capability TLVs in the LDP Initialization message (RFC 5561): P2MP 0x0508, MP2MP 0x0509 and MBB 0x050A. Without the peer's capability, label messages using those FEC elements SHOULD NOT be sent.
sections.eli5: Every tree gets a name tag made of the root's address and a number. Routers also announce 'I know how to build trees' before anyone tries to build one with them.

sections.title: Building a P2MP LSP
sections.content:
A leaf finds its upstream LSR as the LDP peer that is its next hop on the best path to the root, allocates a label L, and sends a Label Mapping <X, Y, L> to that peer. Labels come from the sending LSR's per-platform label space. When several candidates exist, the choice is local, except on a LAN where the RFC recommends a hash, CRC32(Opaque Value) modulo N, over candidates numbered from lower to higher IP address so that all receivers elect the same upstream LSR.

A transit node that receives a mapping, and has no state yet, picks its own upstream LSR, allocates a new label L' and installs a swap from L' to L on the interface toward the sender, then sends <X, Y, L'> upstream. If it already has state, it just adds another outgoing branch and sends nothing new. The root installs state to push label L onto the traffic it maps to the LSP.

Withdrawal works in reverse. A leaf with no downstream neighbors and no need to be egress SHOULD send a Label Withdraw, and a transit node that is left with no state propagates the withdraw upstream. If the upstream LSR changes, the node allocates a new label, copies state and sends a mapping to the new upstream LSR and a withdraw to the old one. If this cannot be atomic, the RECOMMENDED default is to remove the old label before adding the new one.
sections.eli5: Each house asks the road next to it, 'please send me the package', and that road asks the next road, all the way back to the sender. Where two requests meet, the roads share the same path.

sections.title: Building an MP2MP LSP
sections.content:
An MP2MP LSP consists of a downstream path, much like a P2MP LSP from the root, and an upstream path used to send toward the root and the other leaves. Traffic from a downstream node travels up and branches downward as needed, and a packet received from a downstream node MUST never be forwarded back to that same node. A leaf that sends does not receive its own packets.

The messages are named by direction. A leaf sends an MP2MP-D Label Mapping upstream and expects an MP2MP-U Label Mapping in return, which tells it the label to push for traffic it sends. For installing the upstream path, ordered mode SHOULD be used: a node waits for the MP2MP-U mapping from upstream, and the root starts the chain. The benefit is that a leaf that starts sending as soon as its upstream path is installed will have its packets reach the root without being dropped for an incomplete LSP.

Transit and root nodes build the upstream state from the downstream state while omitting the swap toward the node the packet came from, which prevents echoing a packet back to its source. Withdrawals clean up both directions, and an upstream LSR change follows the P2MP procedure.
sections.eli5: An MP2MP tree is a road that works in both directions. Anyone can send up toward the trunk and the message then spreads down to everyone except the person who sent it.

sections.title: Root Redundancy and LAN Optimization
sections.content:
The root node is a single point of failure for an MP LSP, and the problem is particularly severe for MP2MP LSPs, where all leaves must use the same root. The RFC's answer is to define two or more root addresses for the same opaque value and build a tree to each; the network treats them as different MP LSPs.

For P2MP, only one root should forward at a time, to save bandwidth and to avoid duplicate packets, and how the roots decide is out of scope. For MP2MP, a sending leaf picks one root, for example the closest by unicast metric, and MUST forward on only one MP2MP LSP at a time. All leaves MUST join all roots. Convergence is as fast as unicast routing, at the cost of more label resources.

On a LAN, the basic procedure would make the upstream LSR send a copy per receiver. Section 6 uses upstream label allocation (RFC 5331 and RFC 6389) so a packet carries a context label naming the upstream LSR and a second label naming the LSP.

The RFC also notes that unicast micro-loops can create loops in MP LSPs. Loops between two directly connected routers are prevented, but loops among more than two LSRs are not.
sections.eli5: If the one trunk of the tree breaks, nobody gets anything. So you can plant a spare trunk ahead of time and switch to it quickly, though it costs some extra effort to keep both.

sections.title: Make Before Break
sections.content:
When the best path to the root changes, the LSP may break briefly and lose packets. The optional Make Before Break (MBB) procedures keep that loss short by building the new path before dropping the old one. They use the LDP MP Status TLV (type 0x096F) carrying an MBB status value with code 1 for an MBB request and 2 for an MBB ack.

The downstream node allocates a new label, creates an inactive accepting element for the new upstream neighbor, and sends an MBB Label Mapping. It keeps accepting packets on the old label until the new upstream LSR replies with an MBB notification, which it sends only once it is itself connected toward the root. Then the downstream node activates the new element and removes the old one.

If a second change happens first, the older inactive element is removed and a Label Withdraw is sent. A timeout SHOULD be applied in case the notification never arrives, and if the old upstream is seen going down the node can proceed without waiting. A node that has not advertised the MBB capability must not be sent MBB parameters.
sections.eli5: It is like building the new bridge before closing the old one, so cars never have to wait with no road at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same security considerations apply as for base LDP in RFC 5036.

The protocol provides no authorization mechanism for controlling which LSRs may join a given MP LSP. If that is wanted, extra mechanisms outside this document are needed. The RFC points out that such policies cannot be enforced only at the root, because the root does not learn the identities of all the leaf nodes.
sections.eli5: Anyone who is a trusted neighbor router can ask to join a tree, and the sender cannot see everyone who joined. Keeping out the wrong joiners needs extra rules.
